name: numbers/ecmascript-number-form
about: How a number is written when it is hashed (spec 12 §4.2). Two servers that scope an idempotency record differently answer each other's retries with already_exists instead of the first attempt's result, so this is the form both runtimes must agree on, and it is the one a third implementation has to reproduce without reading either.
source: ECMA-262, Number::toString(x, 10). Every expectation below is derived from that algorithm, not captured from a Rayfold runtime: a vector written down from an implementation only proves the implementations agree, which was true the whole time the RB dictionary in spec 09 was wrong.
rule: Let n, k and s be integers such that k >= 1, 10^(k-1) <= s < 10^k, s x 10^(n-k) = x, and k is as small as it can be.
k <= n <= 21: the k digits of s, then n-k zeros. No decimal point, no exponent.
0 < n <= 21: the k digits of s with a decimal point after the first n of them.
-6 < n <= 0: '0.', then -n zeros, then the k digits of s.
otherwise: exponential. One digit, then '.' and the rest when k > 1, then 'e', then the sign of n-1, then |n-1|.
Negative zero is written '0': the sign of zero is not information a hash should carry.

cases.name: zero
negative zero is written as zero
cases.why: String(-0) is '0' in ECMAScript; a scope must not depend on how a client spelled nothing

cases.name: an integer keeps no decimal point
cases.why: JSON parsing gives the value, so the literal 1.0 and the literal 1 are one number

cases.name: a trailing zero is not part of the number
negative
three digits
the same value written with an exponent
cases.why: n = 3, so k <= n <= 21 and the exponent form is not used

cases.name: binary floating point is not hidden
cases.why: the value of 0.1 + 0.2; canonicalisation rounds nothing

cases.name: four decimal places
the last magnitude written in full, small end
cases.why: n = -5, so -6 < n <= 0 holds and the plain form is used

cases.name: the first magnitude written as an exponent, small end
cases.why: n = -6, so -6 < n is false: this is the boundary, and it is exclusive

cases.name: several digits just inside the small boundary
several digits just outside it
the last magnitude written in full, large end
cases.why: n = 21, so k <= n <= 21 holds: 1 followed by twenty zeros

cases.name: the first magnitude written as an exponent, large end
cases.why: n = 22 leaves the plain range; note the '+' on a positive exponent, which the small end does not have

cases.name: many digits just inside the large boundary
cases.why: n = 21; the digits beyond what a double holds are already lost by parsing

cases.name: the largest exact integer
one past it is not representable and rounds
cases.why: the nearest double to 2^53 + 1 is 2^53; a client cannot send the odd number at all

cases.name: more digits than a double carries
the smallest positive number
the largest
